Parties have returned from the scene
of the dreadful massacre at the ranch
of Carlos Machado, near Old Camp
Grant, by the Apache Indians who
recently broke away from the San Car
los reservation. They report that on
their way out from Tucson they met,
near Canada Deloro, q Mexican named
Benito Corillas, who had almost mir
aculously escaped from the massacre,
of which he was the sole survivor. He
was wounded by a bullet-shot through
the wrist. He gave the following mar
rative of the attack, which was wit
messed from distance by poor Macha-
do, who fed with the terrible tidings
to Tucson:


On the morning of the massacre
Corillas and two other men We're at
work near and in front of Machado's
house. They saw Il large number of
Apaches approaching, but at first felt
accustomed to visiting the ranch. On
arriving at the place the Apaches
asked for two of the men employed
there, Romano Esmerdon and Men
doza. They were informed that the
men were away. The Indians then
went into the corral, and formed into
lines like soldiers. Then, for the first
time, Deloro and his companions an
ticipated treachery. They at once
rushed into the house and closed the
doors. The Apaches instantly opened
fire, shooting through the windows,
and almost Immediately killing the
woman and two children. The Indians
then set fire to the house, and with an
axe made hole into the room where
the three men were, and soon smoked
them out. The men retreated into an
other house on the opposite side of the
corral. One, Jesus Nasquez, was killed
soon after getting into the room; and
soon afterward Rafael Romano was
also killed, leaving Corillas, rs the
Apaches thought, their victim certain.
AS soon as Romano fell, COrillas took
his dead comrades gun, and fought
his way through to the river, escaping
death by miracle. He lay secreted
in the brush by the river all day and
night, and then made his escape.
Corillas says the corral was full of
Apaches, but he does not know the
number. The band was led by "Pach-
ero,n who shot Corillas in the wrist,
and who also killed the woman. "A
number of the Old Camp Grant In
dams were recognized among the
band.


The party from Tucson found the
bodies of Machado's wife and two
children, and of the. two men, ana
buried them. The house had been
burned, and every thing on and about
the premises was destroyed except a
few hogs and chickens. Among the
property destroyed or taken was one
Shot gun, a pistol, eighteen head OF
cattle and three horses, large amount
of corn and beans, and all the clothing
and household furniture.

Some say, that ever ,gainst that season comes
Wherein our Saviour's birth is celebrated,


And then, they say, M spirit dares Stir abroad !;
The nights are wholesome; then no planets


strike,


SO hallow'd and so gracious is the time.


Christmas, with its pleasant memo
ries and hallowed associations, has
come again. 1t is time when all
hands are open and charity reigns in
the heart of every one. To-day the
absent ones return and all save those
who have gone up higher are gathered
beneath the old roof tree. Old times
and pleasant scenes come trooping
along the dim avenue of the past.
They are brighter and fresher and
seem to come nearer to-day than of
all the other days of the year. Old
memories and dead hopes are passed
in silent reviews and glancing back
ward toward the dead sea of Oblivion
many, too many, see much to sadden
and too little to gladden. the heart or
cause wish that these rapidly reced-
ing memories might be stayed in their
flight. Christmas, with all it's happy
scenes and merry faces; with all its
noise and mirth and jollity, is yet
suggestive of thought and retrospect
and self-communion. The mind will
float down the River Time" and re-
visit the elsie" of the "Long Ago" 1t
will relight the long closed and funeral
draped rooms of Memory's Chamber,
and our idols, long broken but ever
worshipped, fit before us. The gentle
face-the loved form-of our boyish
dreams, stands out from the faded
canvas, fresh and beautiful as in the
rosy dawn of life's fair morn. Scorned,
blasted, trampled dead affection quick
ems in in its charnel-house, and while
the mind inaudibly repeats, 80, the
dreary, dreary moorland; O, the bar
rem Shore" the heart thrills with the
old but never forgotten joy. Old
times, old scenes and loved faces all
pass again in memory's grand review.
But why recall the past? 1t is gone;
it is beyond our control. To-day is
ours; it is all we have. Let us eat,
drink and be merry, for tomorrow we
die. Man comes into the world, lives,
suffers and gives place to others who
learn the same lessons, thrill with
the same joys, writhe in the same
anguish and disappear from sight
perhaps from memory. Time rolls on
and the day draws near when those
who know us now and, let us hope,
love us, shall wet our graves with their
tears, mourn, then sorrow and finally
be consoled. Christmas should be
happy day. 1t is the anniversary of
the birth of Him who died that we
might live. 1t is the day on which
harmony and good feeling prevails and
all hearts rejoice. In the old time


Twas Christmas broached the mightiest ale;
Twas Christmas told the merriest tale;


Christmas gambol oft would cheer


A poor mans heart through half the year.

Leaving for the Black Hills.


ST. PAUL, Sept S.-A dispatch from
Bismarck says that a party of so men
will leave Bismarck in about thirty
days for the Black Hills. The party
will be composed of experienced min
ers and hunters, who not only know
the color of gold and the habits of the
Indians, but are shaep enough to
evade the military, and who, once in
the Hills, can live as red men, and
consequently not bother themselves
with supplies to any extent.


Arkansas Convention.


LITTLE Rock, Sept. S.-The Consti-
tutional Convention yesterday COM
pleted its new Constitution, which
was signed by all but seven members.
Resolutions deprecating and denounc-
ing outrages in the State and demand
ing equal Justice to all, without regard
to race or color; pledging themselves
to sustain the laws and inviting i'm
migration to the State, were adopted.

EGG HARBOR, Mich, Sept. S.-The

have spread considerably since yester-
day.


Fight with the Indians.


CHICAGO, Sept S.-Lieutenant Gen
eral Sheridan received dispatch to-
night from General Pope, with re-
port from Col. Miles, from his camp
Red River, via Fort Dodge, of a decis-
i've battle with about 500 Comanches
and hostile Indians on the day before,
August 3Oth. Col. Miles command
had been in pursuit of these Indians
ten days, over terribly rough aud
almost impossible country, before
they could be brought to a stand. The
route was strewn with stores which
they had thrown away to aid them In
their flight. The troops fought splen-
didly and the victory was complete.

The Church and the Government.


NEW YORK, Sept s.-A Rome letter
says: In progressing with the seques-
tration of church property, the Gov
ernment Commission take action
which show they are determined to
cut nearer and nearer to the bone, and
leave the formerly well-fed body but
little else than skeleton. The estab-
lishment of the Propaganda was last
week made to feel for the first time
the pressure, and at the first turn of
the screw the Government brought to
the auction block the fine property of
the Mantals, large villa or palace in
an admirable situation above Fran
cati.


NEW YORR, Sept. 9.-The London
papers received to-day contain letter
from the Marquis de Safraga, Charge
d'Atfaires of Carlists, regarding the
shooting of some Republican prison
ers at Piu Olothe. It says that the
Republican soldiers had previously
shot and bayonetted the Carlists
wounded and dying in the hospitals at
Olothe. No one regrets the sanguin-
ary character the war has assumed
more than His Majesty, Don Carlos,
but when the enemy will not respect
the ordinary usages of civilized war
fare, there are no means left for the
Royal Generals to employ but retalia-
ton.


TeIesraphic Cables out of Order.


NEW YORK, Sept. 8.-Market re-
ports from Europe have not been re-
ceived in consequence Of the interrnp-
ton of telegraphic communication.
The French cable is interrupted near
Duxbury and st. Pierre, and the lines
in New Foundland are broken east
and north of Sydney.


A Breeze In Brazil.


NEW YORK, Sept. S.-A Panama
letter received to-day, contains brief
account of the attack of the Brazilian
troops on the religious fanatics under
their leader, Maurer. The troops
numbered 400, and in the fight, which
lasted four hours, they lost forty men,
when the survivors fled, abandoning
their artillery.

Producers are sometimes puzzled to
know why city buyers generally ask
for coarse, well-matured hay, in pref
erence to the more tender and in real
ity more nutritious kinds. The Live
Stock Journal thus enlightens: ''Uity
men feed hay for different purpose

food, while the city man regards grain
as the cheapest food, and only gives
sufficient hay to make bulk in the
stomach, and for the purpose Of health.
Coarse, well-matured timothy serves
this purpose better than the early-cut
and fine grasses. They do not desire
such hay as will tempt the horse to eat
too much of it. Straw would answer
this purpose if cut and mixed with the
grain, about as well. But farmers
should be content with the practice of
the city customer, for it enables them

home consumption

mails in the Geological Gardens were
killed: The quantity of powder ex-
ploded was four tons. The details of
the occurrence show that it's disastrous
effects were widespread. Many trees
were uprooted, and houses located two
miles from the canal were shattered.
Seven persons are yet missing. There
was perfect panic for hours, and it
was not until the cause of the terrific
report was learned that the fears of the
people were allayed. Several died
from fright.

The approaching municipal election
is beginning to attract attention.
Candidates for office are coming to the
surface, and the people are discussing
their merits and qualifications. There
are great many interests that wish
to be served and here and there ring
that wishes to retain its encircling
power. Nearly all California towns
that have attained the age and prop
ulation OF Los Angeles, have passed
through the strangling, crushing pro-
cess resulting from the tightening
folds of the local franchise boa. Our
city has not escaped the too common
fate. She has suffered heavily from
weak, if not dishonest, government.
Her rights have been thrown away,
and her property bartered for song.
Not many years back Los Angeles
was closely wrapped in the folds of the
ring anaconda. She is not so hard
pressed now, and her citizens are de-
termined that they, and not few
leaders with large speculative propen-
stiles, will manage municipal affairs.
We predict that the approaching cleo
tion will be struggle between the
people and the anaconda. The HER
AID takes this occasion to announce
that it will take hand in the fight
and will be found fighting on the side
of the people.

son gave the boys salutes of Chinese

BUYING MIRRoRs.-The total disregard Of
many of our people to the fitness Of things is in
no respect so clearly manifested as in the pur
chase of mirrors. One kind is true in its rehec
ton, the two others are exaggerative. Of the
exaggerative one unduly expands the figure,
and the other unduly elongates it. Hundreds
of mirrors are bought every day without refer
ence to this fact You will find short, squatty
people with mirrors that make them look still
shorter and more squatty; and thin, gaunt
people with looking glasses that pare them
down fully one-half. And thus, through care
lessness and indifference the seeds of dissatis-
faction and distrust are sown, and many happy
homes are broken up, to scatter their broken
hearted contents upon the world. People with
square, expansive faces should select elongating
mirrors, and those who are long and thin faced
should get those which will expand them
Self-opinion is stronger than anything else, and
when our own glass assures us that we look

Lincoln, stating that small party of Sioux ap-
peared on the river bank opposite Fort Berthold

threatening for some time the Berthold Agency.

Arickarees and Mandans who have just returned
from the Indian Territory are wild with excite
ment.

Custer's movements, they are so eager for blood
scalps and revenge but they will not have long to
wait as Custer's cavalry expedition is nearly
ready to leave Fort Lincoln. the final preparations
having been completed by the oficers or the Sew
enth cavalry now in this city. General Custer
expects to move next Sunday, but may start

None of our troops in the Indian country
have been in tighter place this summer than
were those under the command of General
Davidson, at the Wachita Agency, in their
last battle The fight was between the Kiowas
and Naconees and four companies of the Tenth
cavalry. The object OF the Indians was to
destroy the agency and annihilate the garri-
son, and for this purpose they fired the
prairie, and, as our dispatches show, came
soldiers, however, were equal to the work. and
not only with great difficulty extinguished the
fires but repulsed the Indians, inficting
heavy punishment Tie charge of Captain
C1rpenter's company appears to have been the
decisive feature of the action. His gallant
men routed massed column of more than
one hundred and fifty red warriors, who were
about to take up commanding position in
the rear of the United States forces
Had it not been for this movement,
promptly ordered by General Davidson and
ganantly executed, our troops would proba-
bly, have not escaped SO well The Indian loss
was large, but its extent is not ascertained,
owing to their we'll known habit OF carrying
their wounded and dead from the field. 1t
would have been much larger had not friendly
Indians been mingled with the hostile tribes
at the beginning Of the engagement. These
well-behaved red men General Davidson has
succeeded in bringing into his camp, and
fifteen or sixteen hundred Caddos, Wachitas,
Comanches, Tawaconies and Others, have
agreed to return to their former quarters.
This victory places the Wachita Agency in
entire safety, and General Davidson has fol-
lowed it up with energy by sending a flying
column in pursuit Of the scattered foe. Severe
punishment will be inflicted upon those who
are captured, and this is the only way in which
the threatened hostilities near Fort Cobb and
Mcclellan Creek, later in the season, can be
ayerted

Last Thursday afternoon little girl
named Annie Wharty, daughter OF
Michael Wharty, living at 507 Mason
street, died in an epileptic fit. The
usual process of decomposition which
usually follows death was so long de-
ferred that up to last night the parents
and friends of the little girl chung to
the hope that the spirit had not yet
taken its flight, and that she would
again open her eyes and gladden. them
with her smile. But this morning I'M
mistakable signs of decomposition
were observed, and yet the odor which
usually accompanies it is lacking, the
limbs have not become rigid, the eyes
have not assumed a deathlike look,
and different degrees of cold are OBJ
served in different portions of the
body. Although not case of sus-
pended animation, as some had sup
posed, there are yet peculiar features
in the operation of death upon the
body of this child.


A Post reporter visited the house Of
Mr.. Wharty on Mason street, near
Post, this morning. The room in
which the body lay was crowded with
ladies, and two Catholic priests were
present. The body lay on a small
couch, and at the foot of the bed was
a crucific, burning candles and several
boquets. The face of the child was
not covered, and at glance she APP
peared to be sleeping, but at closer
inspection blush and purple discolor-
atoms were seen on the neck and
shoulders. There was flush on the
cheeks, and the ears We're quite red.
One of the priests turned up the eye
lid. The appearance of the eye was
perfectly natural, and was not covered
with film, and lacked the usual
CLASSY appearance they assume after
death. The face of the child was
barely cold. The ankles were quite
cold, but the toes almost warm. Not
the slightest odor was perceptible, and
but for the discoloratiOn Of the neck
and shoulders one would think that
the child merely slept.


The little girl has been subject to
epileptic fits since she commenced
cutting her teeth. The one in which
she died last Thursday lasted for half
an hour before she ceased to breathe.
DR.. Chase was in attendance and pro-
nounced her dead. He advised the
parents to set the funeral for Saturday,
stating that the child being fieshy,
and dying so suddenly, decomposition
would take place rapidly. On Friday
the corps looked natural and life. like,
with no evidences of decay. and the
funeral was postponed until Sunday.
Saturday the body looked even more
life-like, and when the appointed hour
on Sunday came and the friends as
sembled to show their sympathy for
the bereaved parents, the condition of
the corpse had rot changed, and the
funeral was again deferred, and will
not take place until more marked
signs of death make their appearance.

The Territory of Arizona was organ
lied February "A, 1868.


1t contains about 70,000,000 acres.


1t is what may be termed noun
famous region, although there are
also between its hills and mountains.


The principal ranges of mountains
are the San Francisco, Bill Williams,
Mongollon, Sierra Blanca, Sierra
Prieta, Pinal Apache. Cordilleras de
Gila, Natanes, Chiricahua, Dragons,
Santa Rita, Graham, Aztec, Wallapai,
Antelope, Cerbat and Hacquehilla.


The principal peaks are, the San
Francisco, about $4,000 feet above the
level of the sea; the Sierra Blanca,
about $4,000 feet; Bill Williams, about
II 300 feet; and Mount Union, about
10000 feet. The highest mountains
are in Northern Arizona.


The mountain ranges and their foot
hills are covered with pine, oak, cedar,
juniper, poplar and other timber; and
we feel safe in asserting that one-third
of the Territory is timber land. AS
most of this timber is large and of fair
quality, it will, in time, prove vast
source of wealth.


The principal rivers are the Colora-
do, which is navigable for hundreds of
miles; the ella, Salt, Verde, Bonita,
Prieta, San Pedro, Beaver, Santa
Cruz, White, Sipicue, Bill Williams,
and little Colorado. Creeks and
springs are numerous, and water is
found everywhere by digging.


The principal towns are, Yuma,
Ehrenberg and Hardyville, on the Col
orado; Wickenburg, Hassayampa
creek; Prescott, on Granite creek;
Phoenix, on Salt River; Florence,
Pima Villages; Maricopa Wells, and
Adamsville, OH the ella; Tuscon, on
the Santa Cruz; Cerbat, Mineral Park
and Chloride, in Wallapai mining dis
trict.


The Military posts are, Whipple,

Counties-Yayapai, which has a
greater number of white inhabitants,
a larger area, more mountain ranges,
streams, timber and mineral deposits
than any other county i'll the Terri
tory.


Pima-which has the largest town
in the Territory, Tucson, and the larg-
est population, twO-thirds of whom
are MeXieans and semi-civilized In
dams.


Maricopa county lies between Pima
and Yavapai, and is noted for its agri-
cultural productions, which far exceed
those of any other county in the Ter
ritory.


Yuma county contains much choice
farming and grazing lands. Her chief
towns-Yuma and Ehrenberg-have
extensive trade with the people of the
interior.


Mohave county is now gaining rap
idly on her sisters, in wealth and pop
ulation. She has mines, grazing and
farming lands that are among the best
on the continent.


The territory formerly known as
Pah-Ute county, has been handed Ovel

A dangerous malady has made its
appearance among the horses of the
Brooklyn City Railroad Company,
and several fatal cases have occurred.
The disease is termed farcy, and is far
more dangerous than the epizooty,
which so generally prevailed in the
two cities about a year ago. AT the
Third avenue stables the disease has
played considerable havoc. The SYM
toms are swelling Of the leg, and the
breaking out of sores like a button
upon all parts of the animal. From
these sores is discharged a Shiny mat
ter, similar to the CHAMBERS. When
the horses are attacked they become
incapacitated for further duty. Many
horses had to be shot at the stables
named. 1t was supposed the fault lay
in the construction of the old stables,
and new ones were built, but with no
more salutary result. The disease
made its appearance several weeks ago,
but was kept quiet by the company.
4 wash of chloride of lime is used upon
the horses, after which they are wash
ed off with soap and water, and every
NIGHT the stables are smoked with tar.
Whitewash Is also plentifully used.
Mr.. Sullivan, the President of the
railroad company, states that they
believe that they now have the disease
under control, and that it will soon
die out. The stables of the Atlantic
avenue, East New York and Green
wood lines have escaped serious loss
from the malady. Several horses in
private stables in South Brooklyn
have died from the farcy. Mr.
Abrams, a veterinary surgeon, says
that the best treatment for the ami.
mails affected is sulphate of iron. with
hot water and carbolic acid. The
stables should also be literally sprin.
killed. with this solution.-[New York
Herald.

S. ID. Pratt, of Penn Yam, New York,
in an article to the Farmers Club. N.
Y, upon his experience with peach
trees, says:


Remembering Prof. Liebig's theory,
that when vegetable is burned the
part which came from the air in the
process of it's growth returns to the at
mosphere, and the part which came
from the ground is reduced to ashes, 1
came to the conclusion that ashes
would be beneficial when applied to
the roots of the trees. They were
standing in soil strongly inclining to
clay, with turf around them which
had not been removed for several
years. After pruning them properly,
removing every indication of worms,
etc., and washing the body and
branches with soap-suds, began OPP
erations below-first removing the turf
about two feet around the tree; then,
with a garden-pick the ground was
lOosened from six to twelve inches in
depth, taking care not to injure the
large roots. Twenty or thirty quarts
of loose dirt were removed, leaving q
large cavity, shaped like saucer,
with the tree standing in the center.
About one pint Of unleached ashes was
sprinkled about the tree, and upon
this chip manure was placed, nearly
filling the cavity. Another pint Of
ashes was sprinkled upon the fertil-
izer, which was gently pressed down,
and the whole covered with the loose
dirt taken from the cavity, leaving
the surface nearly as it was, excepting
the turf. A young orchard was treated
in similar way. The effect was
wonderful. Plum trees that were Ego
ing to the bad" revived. Peach trees
that had presented small and shriveled
leaves threw out q luxuriant foliage,
cherry trees gave fruit larger and fairer
than ever before"

BY KATE TRUE.
Up in early morning light,
Sweeping, busting, "setting right,''
0iling all the household springs,
Sewing buttons, tying strings,
Telling Bridget what to do,
Mending rips in Johnny's shoe,
Running up and down the stair,
Tying baby in her chair,
Cutting meat and spreading bread,
Dishing out so much per head,
Eating as she can, by chance,
Giving husband kindly glance,
Toiling, working, busy life,


"Smart woman,


Dams wife,
Dan comes home at fall of night,
Home so cheerful. neat and bright,
Children meet him at the door,
Pull him in and look him Ger,
Wife asks How the work has gone 7"
"Busy times with us at home !"
Supper done-Dan reads at ease,
Happy Dan, but one to please
Children must be put to bed
All the little prayers are said;
Little shoes are placed in rows,
Bed clothes tucked DER little tees,
Busy, noisy, wearing life,


Tir woman,


Dams wife.
Dan reads on and falls asleep,
See the woman softly creep;
Baby rests at last, poor dear,
Not a word her heart to cheer,
Mending basket full to top,
Stockings, shirt and little frock,
Tired eyes and weary brain,
Side with darting, ugly pain;
"Never mind, twill pass away"
She must work but never play:
Closed piano, unused books,
Done the walks to easy hooks,
Brightness faded out of life,


Saddened woman,


Dams wife.
Up stairs, tossing to and fro,
Fever holds the woman low;
Children wander, free to play
When and where they will, to-day;
Bridget loiters-dinner's cold,
Dan looks anxious, cross, and old;
Household screws are out of place,
Lacking one dear, patient face,
Steady hands SO weak but true,
Hands that knew just what to do,
Never knowing rest or play,
Folded now-and laid away;
Work of six in one short life,


Shattered woman,


Dan wife.

A precious something for an absent ear

The Irish rihemen arrived yesterday in this

with our Amateur Rifle Club. There was once
time when the American sharpshooter earned
his living by his gun, but now our best marks
men shoot for amusement and renown. But

brilliantly successful at Wimbledon, not
withstanding the unfavorable fact that

nobly vindIcated their country by their
victories over the English. Some of
the best marksmen at Wimbledon will
be present at Creedmoor, and it will take
steady nerve and true eye on the part Of our
American champions to beat them. One
thing is sure, that whether our Irish visitors
hit the bull $ eye or not, they cannot miss a
warm hearty and enthusiastic reception from
the American public The target of hospi-
tallty is too big for any of them to miss.

DETROIT, October 14th.-The Amer
lean Woman's Suffrage Association
commenced its annual meeting here
yesterday. The attendance was mod
erately large. Mrs. Julia Ward Howe
delivered the annual address, after
which the report of the Executive
Committee was read by Mrs. Lucy
Stone Blackwell. These papers brief
ly review the progress made during
the past year toward obtaining the
object of the association. The conciu-
sion is that public sentiment is ad-
vancing in favor of civil rights for
women. Various committees were
appointed, and number of letters
read from distinguished men and
women, among whom were Judge
Kingman, of Wyoming, Bishop
Haven, Judge Smith, of Ohio, Eliza
beth Stuart Phelos, Hon. George w.
Julian, of Indiana, and others. In the
evening public meeting was held,
addressed by Mrs. Howe, Mrs. Liv-
ermore, Miss Eastman, and others.
